profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Salt Lake City - South Valley) is located at 7202 South Campus View Drive, West Jordan, UT 84084. The operator publishes a footprint of 30512 square feet and 1.2 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. This building is one of six Flexential locations serving the Salt Lake City market. Salt Lake City's data center sector is drawn in part by some of the lowest electricity and natural gas rates in the nation, historically around 5 to 6 cents per kilowatt-hour from a mix of natural gas and renewable generation, a cooling-efficient high-desert climate, and Utah's sales-and-use tax exemption for data center equipment purchases at facilities exceeding 150,000 square feet, retroactive to mid-2016, according to industry market analysis. Seismic activity along the Wasatch Front is a real engineering consideration for the region's data centers, mitigated through structural design. Other major operators active in the broader Salt Lake City market include DataBank in Bluffdale, Aligned Data Centers in West Jordan, Novva Data Centers, QTS in Eagle Mountain, Meta, and Oracle, reflecting the area's shift from smaller retail colocation toward larger enterprise, HPC, and hyperscale capacity.

Flexential itself traces to the 1999 founding of ViaWest, which built out a Western US colocation footprint including Utah before merging with the Southeast-focused Peak 10 in 2017 and rebranding as Flexential in 2018; the company is now privately held with GI Partners as controlling sponsor. Utah's data center water use has drawn growing state scrutiny: a bill from Rep. Jill Koford, advanced unanimously by a legislative water panel in November 2025 for the 2026 session, would require data centers to report annual water consumption to the state under a $10,000-per-day fine for non-compliance, with individual figures kept anonymized publicly but available to state water officials. Reporting on the bill cited examples ranging from facilities using up to 5 million gallons a day, more than 12,000 times a typical household's usage, to the NSA's Bluffdale, Utah facility at about 23 million gallons annually, against low-water designs like Novva's reported 85,000 gallons; Koford said state water regulators had previously been left out of data-center water-use oversight, which had been handled mainly through city permitting.

reading.body:
Flexential Salt Lake City - South Valley in West Jordan, Utah, publishes 1.2 MW of IT capacity across 30,512 square feet of technical space, operated by Flexential.

At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise colocation density, that load supports roughly 120 racks. At 40 kW per rack, a density closer to AI training workloads, it supports roughly 30 racks. The operator has not published a per-rack power envelope, so neither figure is the operator's own claim, only what the published megawattage implies under each assumption.

Flexential Salt Lake City - South Valley holds 7 published certifications: SOC 1 Type 2 (audited controls over financial reporting processes), SOC 2 Type 2 (audited controls over security, availability, and confidentiality, tested over time rather than at a point), PCI DSS (the standard required to handle payment card data), ITAR (a specific compliance or security standard), NIST 800-53 (alignment with the federal security control catalog), HITRUST (a healthcare-focused security framework built on top of HIPAA). Together these qualify the facility for regulated workloads spanning security auditing, payments, and healthcare data, though which specific tenants rely on which certification is not disclosed.

Utah has 9 facilities mapped in this site's dataset, of which 8 publish a megawatt figure, totaling 51.69 MW. Flexential Salt Lake City - South Valley contributes 1.2 MW of that total. At that published size it is a small facility relative to what frontier AI training infrastructure requires, which now runs into the tens or hundreds of megawatts, though it may still support inference workloads or smaller-scale AI applications.
